tip: 시험 공부 (siheom gongbu) = studying for an exam; the two nouns stack directly, with no linking word.
Korean 'sees' exams: 시험을 봐요 (siheomeul bwayo = take a test).
시 (si) vs 시간 (sigan): 세 시 (se si) = 3 o'clock, but 세 시간 (se sigan) = 3 hours. Adding 간 (gan) turns clock time into a duration.
잘 거예요 (jal geoyeyo) here is 자다 (jada = sleep), not 잘 (jal = well) – they look identical. 'Will sleep' vs 'well': context decides.
언제 (eonje = when) normally takes no 에: 언제 올 거예요? (eonje ol geoyeyo) = when will you come?
누구 + 가 contracts: 누가 (nuga = who, as the subject).
씨 (ssi) after a name = polite 'Mr/Ms': 수진 씨 (Sujin ssi). Don't attach it to your own name.
Meeting spots take 에서: 앞에서 만날 거예요 (apeseo mannal geoyeyo = we'll meet in front).
걸리다 (geollida) = to take time: 얼마나 걸릴 거예요? (eolmana geollil geoyeyo) = how long will it take?
분 (bun = minutes) takes Sino-Korean numbers: 삼십 분 (samsip bun = 30 minutes).
다 잘 될 거예요 (da jal doel geoyeyo) is a set phrase of reassurance: it'll all work out.
내일 봐요 (naeil bwayo = see you tomorrow): present form, future meaning.
배고파요 (baegopayo = I'm hungry): no pronoun needed, since Korean usually drops "I" when it's clear.
안 (an = not) goes right before the verb, no helper needed: 안 먹었어요 (an meogeosseoyo) = didn't eat. Korean has no "do" for negatives.
점심 먹었어요? (jeomsim meogeosseoyo) doubles as a friendly greeting, like "how's it going?"
목말라요 (mongmallayo = I'm thirsty) is 목 (mok = throat) + 마르다 (mareuda = to be dry).
Questions don't rearrange anything – 저녁 먹었어요? (jeonyeok meogeosseoyo) is the exact statement with rising tone. No "did you" flip.
Two markers, no problem: 이 식당은 (i sikdangeun) sets the topic, 불고기가 (bulgogiga) is the subject – "as for this place, the bulgogi is famous."
뭐가 맛있어요? (mwoga masisseoyo = what's tasty?) is the normal way to ask staff for a recommendation.
집 (jip = house) also means an eatery: 이 집은 (i jibeun) = as for this place.
을/를 (eul/reul) tags the object: 한국 음식을 (hanguk eumsigeul = Korean food). Once tagged it can move around the sentence – the verb just stays last.
있어요 (isseoyo) covers both "there is" and "have": 자리 있어요? (jari isseoyo) is literally "does a seat exist?"
인분 (inbun = serving) takes Sino-Korean numbers: 2인분 reads 이인분 (i-inbun), not native 두 (du). Each counter picks its own number system.
Ordering with 하나 (hana = one) after the dish name is the everyday pattern.
셀프 (selpeu = self-serve): at many Korean restaurants you fetch the water yourself.
도 (do = also) replaces 은/는/이/가: 밥도 (bapdo) = rice too.
저기요 (jeogiyo = excuse me) is a polite way to call restaurant staff.
마리 (mari) counts animals, including whole chickens on menus: 한 마리 (han mari) = one bird.
Korean flips "a bottle of soju": the drink comes first, then number + counter – 소주 한 병 (soju han byeong = soju one bottle).
나오다 (naoda = to come out) is how Koreans say food arrives: 나왔어요 (nawasseoyo).
